newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZFOE launches NZ TWI contract to cool reception.
newsitem.headline: NZFOE launches NZ TWI contract to cool reception.

text.p: The New Zealand Futures and Options Exchange on Thursday said it planned to launch a New Zealand dollar currency index contract based on the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Trade-Weighted Index (TWI).
However, market players greeted the plan to launch it on August 18 less than enthusiastically, saying the exchange had missed the bus by several years.
Some also suggested banks would not support the contract partly because it would take away good margin business.

"It's about two years too late. Then again the banks wouldn't have wanted it because the banks had the franchise in the spot market and they would have lost that franchise," said a senior trader from one Wellington bank.
"They (NZFOE) are fighting an uphill battle against the banks because the banks want their customers to come through them rather than through the futures contract."
"We don't think it will take off in a hurry. We won't be actively supporting it," he said.

Traditionally, currency futures contracts around the world have struggled and the NZFOE's first effort based on the NZ dollar-US dollar launched in 1985 was a fiasco. It was only occasionally traded and abandoned by the exchange last year.
NZFOE Chief Executive Peter Mansell said there was sufficient demand from the financial community to provide the TWI contract.
The TWI is a basket of five major currencies, given weighting based on the amount of trade New Zealand conducts with the countries of those currencies.

"A number of organisations have asked if a contract could be available on an exchange traded basis and centrally cleared," said Mansell. "It would take credit party risk off banks and transfer it to the clearing house."
Some people liked to see a transparent market and execute through whoever they wished, he added.
However, bankers noted that transparency was the last thing some players wanted.

"It would be a good tool for small traders. But when people do these TWI trades they are doing them in 30, 50, 100, 500 millions so there is no way the liquidity is there in the futures," said the fixed interest chief of one fund manager.

"It's a trade that is done in large volumes by sophisticated players who may not particularly desire the mechanism of a futures contract, because of lack of liquidity and because every trade is seen by the world."
Mansell said the TWI was being used as a tool every bit as much as two years ago if not more. "It's absolutely crucial."
But market participants said the market was lopsided now with everyone expecting the TWI to fall, and they doubted a sufficiently balanced futures market could develop.
However, Mansell argued that is just a pricing situation which the market would rebalance.
While Mansell accepted the NZFOE needed the support of a few critical players, he said the new contract would be complementary for spot traders and increase foreign interest.
"Offshore players or potential players have said they would like to see a TWI product and if there was sufficient liquidity they would be reasonably favourable towards using that contract."
It would allow them exposure to New Zealand without having to pick an individual currency which the kiwi is valued against, he said.
"These are people comfortable in dealing with futures whereas they may not wish to enter the OTC market."
Mansell said the NZFOE had to try new products.

"Not all contracts are a success. This is one we believe has a reasonable chance of success because it's an established benchmark. The commodity itself has become indispensible as a tool for monetary policy and the TWI has become a household tool."
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
